2.0.0.en: “And in the second year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar Nebuchadnezzar dreamed dreams, wherewith his spirit was troubled, and his sleep brake from him” [1].

2.0.1.en: Perhaps some may ask how the dream came in the second year of Nebuchadnezzar’s reign and Daniel interpreted it, while he and the three youths were still students in training, who did not stand before the king until the end of the days (Dan 1:18), that is, after three years (Dan 1:5)?

2.0.2.en: A. The expression “three years” may refer here to part of the first year, the second year and part of the third year (compare 2 Kgs 18:9-10; Jer 34:14; Mk 8:31), so that the first year of training includes part of the year of Nebuchadnezzar’s accession to the throne, and the third year part of the year of his second reign by the Babylonian reckoning.

2.0.3.en: B. Some see that the second year here means after the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple and the shattering of Jewish society in 588 or 587 B.C.

2.0.4.en: C. The most probable and most accepted opinion is that what is stated in the first chapter was in the days of Nebuchadnezzar when he was his father Nabopolassar’s assistant in ruling, whereas here the second year of the reign is meant, when he took it over alone. Nebuchadnezzar became a king sharing the throne with his father, as was the custom of many kings at that time. Then he besieged Jerusalem as a co-regent king and commander of the army, then was compelled to leave the siege and enter into the battle of Carchemish with Pharaoh because of his rebellion against him... and his father was still alive. When he returned and besieged Jerusalem in 606 or 605 B.C., when the first deportation took place, his father died and he ruled alone. In this the text agrees with what history records. In other words, Daniel and his companions were being trained in the wisdom of the Chaldeans in the last days of Nebuchadnezzar as a co-regent with his father, and then he stood before him in the second year of his sole reign and after the period of training had ended.

2.0.5.en: St. Jerome says that the second year here is after he had become king not only over the Jews and the Chaldeans but over all the other nations such as Assyria and Egypt. For this reason Josephus says that Nebuchadnezzar dreamed a wonderful dream about future matters after his victory over Egypt.

2.0.6.en: It is stated here that he dreamed “dreams” in the plural, although only one dream is recorded here, but the plural is used because of the many subjects the dream carries, or perhaps the king dreamed many dreams over long periods that carried the same meaning, and the last dream came and stirred confusion in him, so he sent for the magicians and the wise men to ask them about this dream.

2.0.7.en: Why did Nebuchadnezzar not tell the dream to the wise men? St. Jerome answers this question, saying: [The dream remained in the king’s heart like a shadow, I mean, a mere echo or traces of the dream, so that if others recounted the dream before him he could recall what he had seen, and therefore they could certainly not deceive him with lies.] Perhaps what multiplied his confusion was his forgetting of the dream, so he felt the need for someone to remind him of it. God, who gave him the message by the dream, made him forget it to increase his confusion, though people usually disregard the dreams they forget.

2.0.8.en: Perhaps Nebuchadnezzar was thinking about the future of the world and seeking guidance from the gods, so the Lord revealed to him the times of the Gentiles (Lk 21:24). He saw that his rule was collapsing, to be followed by empires that appear and disappear until the Lord reigns eternally. The king realized while dreaming that he was seeing extraordinary things, and that there was a message from the other world directed to him, he knew not what. So when he awoke he forgot the details of the dream; all he knew was that it was a strange dream presented to him from heaven, so he sought someone to remind him of what he had seen and to disclose its secret to him.

2.0.9.en: God, who presented the dream to the king, Himself removed the memory of its details from the king’s mind so that he would be greatly confused and resort to the wise men and soothsayers. This happened later with King Ahasuerus, who was stricken with sleeplessness and could not sleep, and he began to browse the records of the palace so that God might begin to work with him for the salvation of His people from the wicked Haman (Esth 6:1).

2.1.0.en: 2 Then the king commanded to call the magicians, and the astrologers, and the sorcerers, and the Chaldeans, for to shew the king his dreams. So they came and stood before the king. 3 And the king said unto them, I have dreamed a dream, and my spirit was troubled to know the dream. 4 Then spake the Chaldeans to the king in Syriack, O king, live for ever: tell thy servants the dream, and we will shew the interpretation. 5 The king answered and said to the Chaldeans, The word is gone out from me: if ye will not make known unto me the dream, with the interpretation thereof, ye shall be cut in pieces, and your houses shall be made a dunghill. 6 But if ye shew the dream, and the interpretation thereof, ye shall receive of me gifts and rewards and great honour: therefore shew me the dream, and the interpretation thereof. 7 They answered again and said, Let the king tell his servants the dream, and we will shew the interpretation of it. 8 The king answered and said, I know of certainty that ye would gain the time, because ye see that the word is gone out from me, 9 That if ye will not make known unto me the dream, there is but one decree for you: for ye have prepared lying and corrupt words to speak before me, till the time be changed: therefore tell me the dream, and I shall know that ye can shew me the interpretation thereof. 10 The Chaldeans answered before the king, and said, There is not a man upon the earth that can shew the king’s matter: therefore there is no king, lord, nor ruler, that asked such things at any magician, or astrologer, or Chaldean. 11 And it is a rare thing that the king requireth, and there is none other that can shew it before the king, except the gods, whose dwelling is not with flesh. 12 For this cause the king was angry and very furious, and commanded to destroy all the wise men of Babylon.

2.1.1.en: These dreams and their like are examples of the work of Almighty God in secret for the sake of His believers.

2.1.2.en: Tertullian, in his treatise “On the Soul,” distinguishes between dreams according to their three sources:

2.1.3.en: A. Dreams from Satan, which sometimes appear true and useful, but are deceptive.

2.1.4.en: B. Dreams from God, as happened with the pagan Nebuchadnezzar, and that is out of His mercy toward all mankind.

2.1.5.en: C. Dreams that occur as a natural work in the daily life of man, often as a reaction to his behavior; for in the evening, when the inner watchman of the soul is idle, the events of the day appear, with the longings and fears, joys and sorrows they carry, in the form of dreams. Therefore it is said that the hungry man often dreams of bread, and the thirsty man of springs of water.

2.1.6.en: “Then the king commanded to call the magicians, and the astrologers, and the sorcerers, and the Chaldeans, for to shew the king his dreams. So they came and stood before the king” [2].

2.1.7.en: The term “Chaldeans” is used to mean the Babylonians in general, but later it came to be used in a narrow sense to mean the class of the wise men alone.

2.1.8.en: Some liberal critics think that the word “Chaldeans” in the age of Daniel meant the people of Chaldea and not a particular class of them. But A.W. Criswell says that archaeological discoveries have shown the correctness of what the prophet Daniel recorded, for in his time it meant a priestly class serving the god Bel or Baal, and they formed the elite of society.

2.1.9.en: It is clear from this statement that the king felt that the dream carried a divine, heavenly message, for he had dreamed much before and paid no attention, but this time he summoned all the magicians, astrologers, sorcerers and Chaldeans, for terror had come upon him and deprived him of the ability to sleep, and he felt that heaven was declaring to him a grave secret.

2.1.10.en: At first the magicians and soothsayers rejoiced at the king’s summons, for they thought that he was seeking their counsel in some matter, or would tell them a dream for them to interpret to him, and by this they would receive gifts and presents from him. They did not tell Daniel and his friends of the king’s summons, out of greed and envy. The Jews raised the question: Why did Daniel and his friends not go in to the king? St. Jerome presents the answer of the Jews to the question: [When the king promised gifts and presents and great honor, they did not care to stand before him so as to appear blameless, so that they would not seek the wealth of the Chaldeans and their honor. Or the Chaldeans themselves, without doubt, envied the Jews for their reputation and learning, so they went in alone before the king to obtain the rewards for themselves. Afterwards they earnestly asked that those who had denied any hope of glory be with them, to share in resolving a public disaster.]

2.1.11.en: Perhaps the failure to summon Daniel and his companions with the magicians was at the request of the king, who, although he had tested their wisdom and found them ten times better than all the magicians and astrologers that were in his realm (Dan 1:20), had not yet trusted their faithfulness and loyalty to him and to his kingdom, so he did not want to ask them about a matter he felt touched the very being of the kingdom.

2.1.12.en: Whether the magicians were the cause or the king, God permitted this so that they would not be included with the company of the magicians and soothsayers... they had to be distinguished from them because they work by the Spirit of the Lord, not by magic and soothsaying. In any case, their separation from them gave the opportunity for God to be glorified in them and through them.

2.1.13.en: “And the king said unto them, I have dreamed a dream, and my spirit was troubled to know the dream.

2.1.14.en: Then spake the Chaldeans to the king in Syriack,

2.2.0.en: tell thy servants the dream, and we will shew the interpretation” [3-4].

2.2.1.en: The king acknowledged his ignorance of the interpretation of the dream, and his weakness before the message of this dream.

2.2.2.en: When they said to him, “O king, live for ever,” it was not a mere simple greeting, but they saw the signs of anxiety filling his face, so they asked him to be cheerful in a good spirit and to remove all anxiety from his spirit, for they were able to interpret the dream with great certainty.

2.2.3.en: “The king answered and said to the Chaldeans,

2.3.0.en: The word is gone out from me: if ye will not make known unto me the dream, with the interpretation thereof, ye shall be cut in pieces, and your houses shall be made a dunghill” [5].

2.3.1.en: Although they had spoken to him with pride, as those who were confident that they would answer his request, they were surprised that he asked of them what was not within their power, and beyond the limits of their arts and knowledge, if they truly had knowledge or learning.

2.3.2.en: These wise men and magicians were demigods in the eyes of the men of the state and the people. Now they were in an extremely humiliating position, as the natural fruit of arrogance and haughtiness, where they ascribed to themselves what was not theirs.

2.3.3.en: This grave threat revealed the king’s violence and brutality, and also gave the opportunity for the news to spread widely, so God was glorified all the more through His work by the prophet Daniel.

2.4.0.en: “But if ye shew the dream, and the interpretation thereof, ye shall receive of me gifts and rewards and great honour: therefore shew me the dream, and the interpretation thereof” [6].

2.4.1.en: Since the king knew that they were greedy and lovers of vainglory, he promised them abundant gifts and rewards with honor.

2.4.2.en: “They answered again and said, Let the king tell his servants the dream, and we will shew the interpretation of it.

2.4.3.en: The king answered and said, I know of certainty that ye would gain the time, because ye see that the word is gone out from me,

2.4.4.en: That if ye will not make known unto me the dream, there is but one decree for you:

2.4.5.en: for ye have prepared lying and corrupt words to speak before me, till the time be changed:

2.5.0.en: therefore tell me the dream, and I shall know that ye can shew me the interpretation thereof” [7-9].

2.5.1.en: The magicians insisted that he tell them the dream, and in arrogance affirmed their ability to interpret it. The king added to the magicians a new crime, the crime of deceit, or agreeing on lying and corrupt words. For since they knew that he had forgotten the dream, and were sure of it, they asked him to relate it to them. He was certain that they were gaining time, perhaps that he might calm down from his rage and pardon them. In the dialogue between the king and the Chaldeans it appears that he was doubtful of them, that they offer honeyed words but are not truthful in knowledge. They tried to gain time so that the wave of his anger might subside and he change his mind about killing them. The word “gain” came to mean “buy,” that is, they buy the time in which there is rage and anger until it passes and ends.

2.5.2.en: The Chaldeans realized that the affairs of the future are declared by God alone. We thank God for His love, for the Word of God has come to us to tell us all things, as the Samaritan woman said: “I know that Messias cometh, which is called Christ: when he is come, he will tell us all things” (Jn 4:25).

2.5.3.en: “The Chaldeans answered before the king, and said,

2.5.4.en: There is not a man upon the earth that can shew the king’s matter:

2.6.0.en: therefore there is no king, lord, nor ruler, that asked such things at any magician, or astrologer, or Chaldean” [10].

2.6.1.en: They offered the king a just excuse, which is that what he asks is not within the power of any man on earth, and history has not recorded a single example of one in authority who asked that someone tell him what he had seen in his dream. Thus all gave a collective testimony that if anyone tells him the dream, this will not be a human work but a divine gift from heaven, for God alone knows the dreams of men and their hidden thoughts. They gave this as a testimony to the God of Daniel before Daniel uttered a word.

2.7.0.en: “And it is a rare thing that the king requireth, and there is none other that can shew it before the king, except the gods, whose dwelling is not with flesh” [11].

2.7.1.en: Some think that they mean here the angels, as being alone able to present this strange dream, which came as a divine revelation and was erased from the king’s mind for a divine purpose, without the disturbance leaving his spirit. Some scholars see that he means the gods, for the Chaldeans worshipped a multitude of gods, with a supreme god who is the sole ruler.

2.8.0.en: “For this cause the king was angry and very furious, and commanded to destroy all the wise men of Babylon” [12].

2.8.1.en: The king was not comforted by the answer of the magicians, but his anger was kindled all the more and his threat turned into a royal decree issued to kill all the wise men of Babylon.

2.9.s.en: 3. The command to slay the wise men:

2.9.0.en: “And the decree went forth that the wise men should be slain;

2.9.1.en: and they sought Daniel and his fellows to be slain” [13].

2.9.2.en: Daniel and his friends were not summoned when the wise men were called by the king to disclose the dream and its interpretation, but when the command to kill the wise men was issued they were sought to be killed with them, and yet they bore no grudge or hatred against them, but Daniel rescued them without a single word of reproach.

2.10.0.en: 14 Then Daniel answered with counsel and wisdom to Arioch the captain of the king’s guard, which was gone forth to slay the wise men of Babylon: 15 He answered and said to Arioch the king’s captain, Why is the decree so hasty from the king? Then Arioch made the thing known to Daniel. 16 Then Daniel went in, and desired of the king that he would give him time, and that he would shew the king the interpretation. 17 Then Daniel went to his house, and made the thing known to Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, his companions: 18 That they would desire mercies of the God of heaven concerning this secret; that Daniel and his fellows should not perish with the rest of the wise men of Babylon.

2.10.1.en: “Then Daniel answered with counsel and wisdom to Arioch the captain of the king’s guard, which was gone forth to slay the wise men of Babylon:

2.10.2.en: He answered and said to Arioch the king’s captain, Why is the decree so hasty from the king?

2.10.3.en: Then Arioch made the thing known to Daniel” [14-15].

2.10.4.en: It is clear from the text that some of the wise men were killed before Daniel and his colleagues were sought to be killed. This killing, together with the publication of the royal decree, had its effect on all circles in the state.

2.10.5.en: When Daniel was sought to be killed, he met the captain of the king’s guard and not the king himself, because he was under sentence of death by the decree issued without any exception, so he needed the intervention of a mediator between them to make clear to the king that the decree included Daniel, though he had not been summoned with the magicians to disclose the dream. For the command to kill him carried injustice with haste. This is clear from the words of gentle and balanced reproach directed by Daniel to the king: “Why is the decree so hasty from the king?!”

2.10.6.en: It is clear from Daniel’s talk with the captain of the guard that Daniel asks what is for the king’s benefit more than in defense of his temporal life. The sudden sentence of his death unjustly did not take away his wisdom and balance and did not disturb his spirit. The dream disturbed the king’s spirit, while the issuing of an order to kill did not confuse Daniel’s mind, for no reason but that Daniel’s life, thought and heart are under the leadership of the Spirit of God. This appears most clearly in his asking the king for a respite to enjoy a divine revelation. He asks with confidence and certainty that the grace of God supports him and provides for his needs. He knew that this request had its danger, for if he returned the next day without an answer his punishment would be doubled, as the king would hasten to kill him, perhaps in a more violent and shameful way, and his case would be made public.

2.10.7.en: “Then Daniel went in, and desired of the king that he would give him time, and that he would shew the king the interpretation.

2.11.0.en: Then Daniel went to his house, and made the thing known to Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, his companions: that they would desire mercies of the God of heaven concerning this secret; that Daniel and his fellows should not perish with the rest of the wise men of Babylon” [15-18].

2.11.1.en: The Chaldeans asked to know the dream in order to interpret it, whereas what Daniel asked for was a short respite of time to stand before the Revealer of secrets and be granted the secret.

2.11.2.en: The statement “Daniel went to his house” indicates that the king gave him a respite of time to prepare himself for the meeting with him, perhaps for one day. Without doubt the king wanted a quick reply to know his dream and remove the disturbance of his spirit, but Daniel most likely asked for this day to enjoy a divine revelation that would disclose to him the dream and its interpretation, and the king granted him the respite.

2.11.3.en: When the king gave him the respite, he did not resort to the library to read, nor to his friends to seek counsel, but he went to them to support him with prayers. Daniel was close to God, yet he felt the need for the prayers and intercessions of his friends before God; thus the Apostle Paul used to ask the people to pray for him that the Lord might give him wisdom at the opening of his mouth. Thus the trial led him and his friends into deeper prayers and fellowship with God.

2.11.4.en: * Daniel asked for time not to search into hidden things with the skill of his mental power, but to seek the Lord of hidden things. For this reason he asked Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah to join him in the request, to avoid the appearance of showing that he alone deserved this, and since they shared in the common danger they shared in a common prayer.

2.12.0.en: St. Jerome. When Daniel spoke with his friends he called God “the God of heaven” [18], and did not say “the God of Israel,” because he knew that Israel had sinned and was no longer worthy for God to be ascribed to it because of its disobedience, but He is ascribed to heaven, which in love submits to His will. This title was used in the books of Nehemiah, Ezekiel and Daniel, as books connected with the captivity, so it appears as though God had departed from His people for a time, so that they might offer collective repentance and He would return and dwell in their midst; this title is also mentioned in the Book of Revelation, where it lifts our hearts to heaven, so that we see our God carrying us to His heavens, and He is called the God of heaven.

2.12.1.en: The three youths supported Daniel with their prayers not out of greed to share a reward from the king with him, nor to remove disgrace from him, but that God might be glorified in His prophet in the land of captivity.

2.12.2.en: The eyes of these godly men were turned toward the divine “mercies,” for they alone are our support in the time of distress.

2.13.0.en: 19 Then was the secret revealed unto Daniel in a night vision. Then Daniel blessed the God of heaven. 20 Daniel answered and said, Blessed be the name of God for ever and ever: for wisdom and might are his: 21 And he changeth the times and the seasons: he removeth kings, and setteth up kings: he giveth wisdom unto the wise, and knowledge to them that know understanding: 22 He revealeth the deep and secret things: he knoweth what is in the darkness, and the light dwelleth with him. 23 I thank thee, and praise thee, O thou God of my fathers, who hast given me wisdom and might, and hast made known unto me now what we desired of thee: for thou hast now made known unto us the king’s matter. 24 Therefore Daniel went in unto Arioch, whom the king had ordained to destroy the wise men of Babylon: he went and said thus unto him; Destroy not the wise men of Babylon: bring me in before the king, and I will shew unto the king the interpretation.

2.13.1.en: God permitted Daniel to be in distress so that he would enter his house and meet the God of heaven, and lift his heart and mind to heaven, and discover deeper secrets, and enjoy a knowledge that fills his being with a sweetness that swallows up every distress. How we need to enter every day into our house, our inner Jerusalem, to meet the One who lifts us from the cares of this life and brings us into the earnest of eternity.

2.13.2.en: “Then was the secret revealed unto Daniel in a night vision.

2.13.3.en: Then Daniel blessed the God of heaven” [19].

2.13.4.en: Since Daniel and his companions asked the Lord without doubting, God granted them the desire of their heart, and as the Apostle James says: “But let him ask in faith, nothing wavering. For he that wavereth is like a wave of the sea driven with the wind and tossed. For let not that man think that he shall receive any thing of the Lord” (Jas 1:6-7). God is near to those who cry to Him in truth and sincerity with faith.

2.13.6.en: Blessed be the name of God for ever and ever: for wisdom and might are his:

2.13.7.en: When God revealed the secret to Daniel, he did not think of his meeting with the king, nor was he preoccupied with what he had received, but offered a new hymn of praise to the Lord, ascribing to God the wisdom he had received and the strength he enjoyed. He glorifies God, who holds history in His hand, and from whom nothing is hidden, and these are two matters that are inseparable when the majesty of God is declared.

2.13.8.en: And he changeth the times and the seasons: he removeth kings, and setteth up kings:

2.14.0.en: he giveth wisdom unto the wise, and knowledge to them that know understanding” [20-21].

2.14.1.en: Many acknowledge the existence of God and His power and wisdom but count Him isolated from the life of mankind in general, and from their own life in particular; but Daniel praises God, who works in the life of all, by His mercy from on high. If there are men who are strong in work and wise, God alone is the source of strength and wisdom, and does not deprive us of them. Our Christ is the wisdom of God, as the Apostle says: “To God only wise, through Jesus Christ” (Rom 16:27); we acquire Him and so acquire wisdom.

2.14.2.en: Contemporary man each morning expects continual changes on the world level, reads the newspapers eagerly, awaiting what is new. But the children of God, each morning, have their hearts lifted to see and perceive God’s plan for the salvation of the world, He in whose hand are all the minutes of events at all levels: worldwide, local, ecclesiastical and personal. Each morning they praise God for His surpassing providence, ever shining with continuous work. The believer sees constant movement in heaven as in nature and in the life of mankind and in his own private life. All of it praises God, who alone is wise and almighty. As for the statement “he giveth wisdom unto the wise,” it means that God gave man natural wisdom, and it is a divine gift. If he is faithful in this natural wisdom, ascribing it to God in a spirit of humility, He grants him a greater heavenly wisdom, and so also with knowledge, for if we are faithful in little, much is given to us; for whoever has, to him will be given, and he will have more abundance.

2.14.3.en: “He revealeth the deep and secret things:

2.15.0.en: he knoweth what is in the darkness, and the light dwelleth with him” [22].

2.15.1.en: He speaks here in particular of the grace of prophecy, where God counts His prophets the interpreters of His secrets to the children of men. This is a grace given to some faithful chosen ones, according to what is for the edification of the community and the declaration of the glory of God.

2.15.2.en: Since God dwells in the light, He brings His men into the light, destroying the kingdom of the devil, that is, darkness. How great is the difference between the magicians, sons of darkness, and Daniel, son of light!

2.15.3.en: St. Augustine distinguishes between the enjoyment of discovering the vision by the spirit and the understanding of the vision by the mind. As we worship God with the spirit and with the mind (1 Cor 14:15), so the prophet Daniel perceived the divine vision by his spirit and discovered its understanding by his mind.

2.15.4.en: * The greatest of the prophets is he who is granted both gifts, I mean the vision by the spirit of the symbolic likenesses of material things, and the understanding of these things by the vital power of the mind.

2.15.5.en: Such was Daniel, whose lofty position was tested and established not only when he told the king the dream he had seen but also explained its meaning (Dan 2:27; 4:16-24). The material images themselves (the dream) appeared to him by the spirit, and the understanding of them was declared to him by his mind. I am using here the word “spirit” in the same sense in which Paul uses it when he distinguishes between the spirit and the mind.

2.16.0.en: St. Augustine. “I thank thee, and praise thee, O thou God of my fathers, who hast given me wisdom and might, and hast made known unto me now what we desired of thee: for thou hast now made known unto us the king’s matter” [23].

2.16.1.en: Daniel glorifies God, “the God of his fathers,” that is, the God of the living Church extending through the ages. The God who worked wonders of old with his fathers now works with Daniel, and works in successive ages to the end of the age. St. Clement of Alexandria says: [God is the giver of wisdom, learning, knowledge and true philosophy.]

2.16.2.en: * The Holy Bible calls every secular learning or art wisdom, and counts artistic invention and skill as being from God. This is clear when we cite the following passage: “And the LORD spake unto Moses, ‘See, I have called by name Bezaleel the son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah: and I have filled him with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge’” (Ex 31:1-2).

2.16.3.en: Those who are wise in mind have a special strength by nature ascribed to them, and those who show themselves able to receive from “the wisdom of the Most High” have a spirit of double understanding.

2.16.4.en: * God gives wisdom from His own mouth, and knowledge with understanding, and lays up help for the righteous.

2.16.5.en: * Before the coming of the Lord, philosophy was necessary for the Greeks for righteousness. And now it leads man to godliness, as a kind of training which prepares those who have reached faith through proof.

2.16.6.en: St. Clement of Alexandria. “Therefore Daniel went in unto Arioch, whom the king had ordained to destroy the wise men of Babylon:

2.16.7.en: he went and said thus unto him;

2.16.8.en: Destroy not the wise men of Babylon:

2.17.0.en: bring me in before the king, and I will shew unto the king the interpretation” [24].

2.17.1.en: Why did Daniel ask Arioch to stop killing the wise men though they were magicians and behaved as followers of Satan?

2.17.2.en: A. He did not ask this because they were righteous, but because the sentence to kill them was issued unjustly, since no one can know dreams except God alone.

2.17.3.en: B. They were not Jews who had heard the Law that forbids magic and soothsaying.

2.17.4.en: C. By the stopping of their killing He gives them, their families and their acquaintances the opportunity to realize the true work of God in the life of His prophets.

2.17.5.en: God quickly answered the prayers of Daniel and his companions, and Daniel did not forget to thank God before going forward to the king and telling him the dream and its interpretation. Daniel, in captivity, felt the surpassing care of God; God, the Ruler of all, determines the appointed times and seasons. For centuries later the Lord Christ came, and the Jewish leaders took care not to seize Him and kill Him at a feast for fear of the gathering of the people. Yet the plan of God was accomplished by His being killed during the Passover feast, to affirm that He is the true Passover, in whom the types of the feasts were fulfilled.

2.17.6.en: St. Hippolytus of Rome comments on the disclosure of the secret to Daniel, saying: [The dream remained a secret for those whose thought is earthly, but for those who seek the heavenly things, the heavenly secrets are declared.] [God showed them that what is impossible for man is possible for God.]

2.17.7.en: St. Hippolytus of Rome sees that the name Arioch means literally “chief of the butchers” or “chief of the cooks.”

2.18.0.en: 25 Then Arioch brought in Daniel before the king in haste, and said thus unto him, I have found a man of the captives of Judah, that will make known unto the king the interpretation. 26 The king answered and said to Daniel, whose name was Belteshazzar, Art thou able to make known unto me the dream which I have seen, and the interpretation thereof? 27 Daniel answered in the presence of the king, and said, The secret which the king hath demanded cannot the wise men, the astrologers, the magicians, the soothsayers, shew unto the king; 28 But there is a God in heaven that revealeth secrets, and maketh known to the king Nebuchadnezzar what shall be in the latter days. Thy dream, and the visions of thy head upon thy bed, are these; 29 As for thee, O king, thy thoughts came into thy mind upon thy bed, what should come to pass hereafter: and he that revealeth secrets maketh known to thee what shall come to pass. 30 But as for me, this secret is not revealed to me for any wisdom that I have more than any living, but for their sakes that shall make known the interpretation to the king, and that thou mightest know the thoughts of thy heart.

2.18.1.en: “Then Arioch brought in Daniel before the king in haste, and said thus unto him,

2.18.2.en: I have found a man of the captives of Judah, that will make known unto the king the interpretation” [25].

2.18.3.en: Arioch presented Daniel to the king as one who had done the king a good turn deserving a reward, for he says to him: “I have found a man...” whereas Daniel ascribed nothing to himself, but gave all the glory to God.

2.18.4.en: Daniel had already gone in to the king and asked him for a respite to present the secret to him, so why does Arioch present him as though the king had no knowledge of Daniel’s case? Perhaps because the king had given Daniel a respite of one day, but in his friendly talk with Arioch he showed his despair that Daniel or any of the other wise men could know the secret, counting that the day’s respite he had granted Daniel was only to justify his justice in killing all the wise men including Daniel.

2.18.5.en: “The king answered and said to Daniel, whose name was Belteshazzar,

2.19.0.en: Art thou able to make known unto me the dream which I have seen, and the interpretation thereof?” [26].

2.19.1.en: It is clear from this question the king’s despair of there being a man able to discover the dream and know its interpretation. The king spoke with Daniel affirming the impossibility of accomplishing the matter, and this glorified God all the more, and showed His surpassing work with Daniel.

2.19.2.en: “Daniel answered in the presence of the king, and said,

2.19.3.en: The secret which the king hath demanded cannot the wise men, the astrologers, the magicians, the soothsayers, shew unto the king;

2.19.4.en: But there is a God in heaven that revealeth secrets, and maketh known to the king Nebuchadnezzar what shall be in the latter days.

2.20.0.en: Thy dream, and the visions of thy head upon thy bed, are these” [27-28].

2.20.1.en: At the beginning of his talk with the king he made clear that the dream was prophetic, confirming the king’s idea that the dream was not an ordinary dream at all. Since the dream was neither natural nor human, therefore no man can disclose or interpret it, but God, who gave the king the dream by His Spirit, reveals His secret.

2.20.2.en: God granted him a revelation of what shall be in the latter days, when every king falls and another rises in his place, until the King of kings comes and establishes His spiritual kingdom in hearts.

2.21.0.en: “As for thee, O king, thy thoughts came into thy mind upon thy bed, what should come to pass hereafter: and he that revealeth secrets maketh known to thee what shall come to pass” [29].

2.21.1.en: Daniel stirred the king’s feelings all the more when he told him that his dream was not a natural dream but an ascent of his thoughts and a lifting of them to enjoy the presence of God, the Revealer of secrets, who endowed him with this dream.

2.21.2.en: “But as for me, this secret is not revealed to me for any wisdom that I have more than any living,

2.22.0.en: but for their sakes that shall make known the interpretation to the king, and that thou mightest know the thoughts of thy heart” [30].

2.22.1.en: God in His wisdom lifted the king’s thoughts to enjoy a special secret concerning the last days, but he could not understand the dream; as for Daniel, he did not receive the dream, but received the knowledge of the king’s dream and the knowledge of its interpretation. Daniel did not ascribe to himself wisdom or knowledge above other children of men, but gives glory to God who reveals the secret to him, lest the king be enraged and sin against God, who gave him the dream and then removed its memory from him and did not give him the interpretation. Daniel said: The God who gave you the dream gave you me as an interpreter of the dream. It is as though all that happens is by a well-ordered divine plan.

2.22.2.en: Perhaps someone asks: Does God speak to us now by dreams? He is able to do so, but He gives us what is greater, for Paul says: “Hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son” (Heb 1:2).

2.23.0.en: 31 Thou, O king, sawest, and behold a great image. This great image, whose brightness was excellent, stood before thee; and the form thereof was terrible. 32 This image’s head was of fine gold, his breast and his arms of silver, his belly and his thighs of brass, 33 His legs of iron, his feet part of iron and part of clay.

2.23.1.en: “Thou, O king, sawest, and behold a great image.

2.23.2.en: This great image, whose brightness was excellent, stood before thee; and the form thereof was terrible” [31].

2.23.3.en: Perhaps some ask: Why did God present this dream, concerning the four kingdoms that end with the coming of the Lord Christ, to Nebuchadnezzar and not to Daniel?

2.23.4.en: A. Had the dream been presented to Daniel and he had declared it and declared its interpretation, all the Jews scattered in the Babylonian state, and also the remnant left in Israel, would not have heard of it. But since it was declared to the king, whose spirit was troubled and who almost killed all the wise men, magicians and soothsayers, the matter spread through the whole kingdom, and every Jew was able to ask about the divine secret behind this dream.

2.23.5.en: B. Since the dream concerns the coming of the Lord Christ, the Savior of the world, He wanted the Gentiles to hear of it, that they might follow the matter of the coming of the Savior.

2.23.6.en: “This image’s head was of fine gold,

2.23.7.en: his breast and his arms of silver,

2.23.8.en: his belly and his thighs of brass,

2.24.0.en: his feet part of iron and part of clay” [32-33].

2.24.1.en: After Daniel presented the dream he did not ask: “Is this the dream?” but in confidence and certainty that what God had declared to him was true he said: “This is the dream?” The king was listening to him in silence with astonishment, for Daniel had told him the dream with great accuracy.

2.24.2.en: The following is observed in this dream: 1. The king saw a great royal image; in the original it is “one great image,” for despite the difference of its metals it is one image. All the successive kingdoms, despite the difference of their capabilities, in the sight of God are one image, or one temporal power, very splendid in the eyes of those who benefit from it, and terrifying (terrible) to those who fall under the pressure of these powers. The king did not see many images or statues but one image, although the four kingdoms differ from one another, indeed each kingdom arose on the ruins of the other. Persia arose by its victory over Babylon, and Macedonia at the expense of Persia, and the Roman state at the expense of Macedonia. Despite the difference of these kingdoms they share in their resistance to the will of God, and so they represent one unit resisting the truth. 2. The head of the image is of gold, and it ends with feet of iron and clay, and in this is an indication of the gradual decline of the world and its weakness and increasing corruption through the generations. 3. Here he speaks of each kingdom as a whole, and not of particular kings. For if Cyrus was found to bear noble qualities with wisdom and balance, yet the kingdom of Persia as a whole bears corruption and resistance to the truth. 4. This dream was presented to a pagan king, so that when the captive Jews who long to return to their country come to know it, they will not be seized by despondency when the kingdom of Persia appears to rule Babylon, and then the Greeks, and then the Romans, and in all this Israel no longer appears as in the days of King David or Solomon, because God wanted to present the kingdom of the Son of David, the stone that strikes the image and becomes a great mountain, whose spiritual kingdom extends over the whole world!

2.24.3.en: He wanted to turn their eyes from awaiting a temporal kingdom to an eternal spiritual Kingdom. 5. He ignored the kingdom of Assyria, because the dream is not meant to record history but to lead all toward the Lord Christ, the Savior of the world. Therefore he did not mention the previous kingdoms, but began with the kingdom of Babylon. 6. Nebuchadnezzar is described in this dream and this vision as “the head of gold,” for he is the one who made Babylon a world empire with its glory, greatness, sovereignty and authority; therefore the divine inspiration made him not only the founder of this empire but pictured him as being one with Babylon, for he was a symbol of it and a representative of its greatness, as in his saying: “Is not this great Babylon, that I have built for the house of the kingdom by the might of my power, and for the honour of my majesty?” (Dan 4:30), or as the inspired word described him: “It is thou, O king, that art grown and become strong: for thy greatness is grown, and reacheth unto heaven, and thy dominion to the end of the earth” (Dan 4:22). Nebuchadnezzar was a king, a military commander, a builder and a singular genius, and his authority was direct and without limit over all who submitted to his scepter.

2.24.4.en: The divine inspiration symbolized this king and his kingdom by gold, which in the Holy Bible symbolizes greatness, exaltation and loftiness. The kingdom was also famous for the abundance of gold in it. Herodotus, who visited Babylon about 90 years after Nebuchadnezzar (450 B.C.), says that he had not seen gold on earth in such abundance as he saw in Babylon, especially in its temples, shrines, altars, vessels and equipment, and other historians related what they saw of articles of pure gold. 7. He symbolized the kingdom of Persia and Media by silver, which in the Holy Bible refers to wealth and the continual pursuit of money: “He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied” (Eccl 5:10), as Judas sold the Lord Christ for silver (Lk 22:5). The word “silver” in all the Semitic languages was the same word as “money.” This empire was very fond of money and developed an extensive system of taxes which were paid in silver, and because of this tax system the kings of Media and Persia gathered a vast store of silver funds. The prophet Daniel prophesied in his third vision (Dan 11:2) about one of the kings of the Persians who “shall be far richer than they all,” and he meant Ahasuerus, who gathered all the silver of his father Darius and the other kings of Persia.

2.24.5.en: “Thou, O king, art a king of kings: for the God of heaven hath given thee a kingdom, power, and strength, and glory.

2.24.6.en: And wheresoever the children of men dwell, the beasts of the field and the fowls of the heaven hath he given into thine hand, and hath made thee ruler over them all.

2.24.7.en: Thou art this head of gold” [37-38].

2.24.8.en: The phrase “king of kings” was a title used for many rulers of the East, for the cuneiform inscriptions have shown that it was a common title among the Persians, and among the Ethiopians and Babylonians. Nebuchadnezzar is also given the title “king of kings” in the book of Ezekiel (Ezek 7:25), and his authority extended over the whole civilized world of his time, especially the historic nations such as Egypt, Palestine and Asia Minor. In this sense Babylon became a world kingdom, and was the first model and beginning as representative of all the world powers that followed it.

2.24.9.en: It is observed here that Daniel did not flatter the king but called him the golden head of the image which is utterly shattered, and that after him another kingdom would arise. And when he says “Thou art this head” he does not mean him personally but the kingdom of Babylon, one of whose most famous kings was Nebuchadnezzar. This king was known for cruelty and violence, as King Belshazzar was known for his disdain of the true God.

2.25.0.en: “And after thee shall arise another kingdom inferior to thee, and another third kingdom of brass, which shall bear rule over all the earth” [39].

2.25.1.en: He called the kingdom of Persia inferior to the kingdom of Babylon, not in respect of breadth of territory nor weakness of power and authority or wealth, but it is inferior because of increasing corruption and brutality. Even Cyrus, who was balanced and wise in some matters, used brutality as he tried to dominate the whole world in every direction.

2.25.2.en: He then speaks of the kingdom of the Macedonians, which ruled over all the earth, and calls it “of brass,” not because it was harder than the kingdom of Persia, but because it was baser, so that when compared with it, it is like brass compared with silver.

2.25.3.en: “And the fourth kingdom shall be strong as iron: forasmuch as iron breaketh in pieces and subdueth all things: and as iron that breaketh all these, shall it break in pieces and bruise.

2.25.4.en: And whereas thou sawest the feet and toes, part of potters’ clay, and part of iron, the kingdom shall be divided; but there shall be in it of the strength of the iron, forasmuch as thou sawest the iron mixed with miry clay. And as the toes of the feet were part of iron, and part of clay, so the kingdom shall be partly strong, and partly broken.

2.25.5.en: And whereas thou sawest iron mixed with miry clay, they shall mingle themselves with the seed of men: but they shall not cleave one to another, even as iron is not mixed with clay” [40-43].
